stories.headline: Absconding in UP bizman murder case, accused model Shraddha Dubey may be in Nepal
stories.deck: The investigation into Shiva Sharma's death has led authorities to search for Shraddha Dubey across borders. CCTV footage reportedly shows Shraddha, her sister Rashmi, and an associate Adil in Nepal. They are believed to have fled Lucknow soon after the incident, raising suspicion. Sharma's family has alleged foul play, while Dubey maintains her innocence and claims he died by suicide.
stories.bodyText:
LUCKNOW: The search for absconding model-influencer Shraddha Dubey, the prime accused in the Shiva Sharma death case, has widened beyond India, with police following leads that place her in Nepal.
Photographs circulating on social media and CCTV visuals said to show Shraddha with her sister Rashmi and an associate Adil have become the latest focus of scrutiny as police attempt to trace the trio’s route after Sharma’s death.
The trio was last traced to Mahim Nagar in Nepal, where CCTV cameras recorded them crossing a road and entering a bus station.
Sources said they stayed at the facility overnight and left by bus the next morning, departing before cops could reach the spot. Police have not issued an official confirmation of the identities of the people seen in the footage, and verification of the visuals remains part of the ongoing inquiry.
The reported Nepal trail has added a new dimension to the probe into the death of a 28-year-old businessman and restaurateur.
Sharma died after falling from the fourth floor of an apartment building in Lucknow on Oct 9. His family has alleged foul play and accused Shraddha and others of involvement, allegations she has denied in public statements. 
Police believe the accused may have fled Lucknow soon after the incident.
A key lead emerged when a Scorpio SUV linked to Shraddha, bearing registration number UP 32 QQ 0111, was found parked at a private parking in Rupaidiha in Bahraich district on Oct 10. The location, close to the India-Nepal border, strengthened suspicions that those sought may have crossed into Nepal after abandoning the vehicle.
Police teams have been deployed at multiple locations to trace Shraddha, Rashmi and the third accused, while officials work to reconstruct their movements based on footage, photographs and other inputs.
Lucknow Police have announced a reward of 25,000 for information leading to Shraddha’s arrest.
Even as the search continues, Shraddha Dubey has posted multiple videos on social media asserting her innocence. She has claimed Sharma died by suicide and urged that she not be linked to politicians, bureaucrats or influential individuals on the basis of speculation.
She alleged Sharma was under heavy financial stress, citing debts of 15 lakh to 20 lakh, and said investigators should examine CCTV footage, mobile data and call detail records.

stories.headline: US start-up plans to sell sunlight at night with help from India’s Skyroot Aerospace
stories.bodyText: Washington: An American space technology company plans to sell on-demand sunlight at night at precise locations on Earth by placing massive reflecting mirrors in orbit, using launch services from India's Skyroot Aerospace. California-based Reflect Orbital plans to launch a constellation of satellites to provide on-demand sunlight for services such as illuminating disaster zones for search and rescue operations and extending power generation at solar farms. The start-up has signed a contract with Hyderabad-based Skyroot Aerospace for two launches onboard its Vikram rockets. "These launches give us assured schedule and capacity alongside our other planned launches from US sites," Reflect Orbital said in a statement. "Excited to partner with Reflect Orbital, pioneering one of the most innovative ways to harness space technology to unlock new possibilities here on Earth! Looking forward to launching their vision of sunshine on demand with @SkyrootA rockets," Skyroot Aerospace CEO Pawan Chandana said in a post on X. . In July, the company received approval from the Federal Communications Commission to construct, launch and operate a demonstration satellite. The start-up aims to provide on-demand sunlight that can be turned off anytime with adjustable brightness over a five-km swathe. The company says that on-demand sunlight can help extend work hours in remote industrial zones, aid defence operations by lighting up critical infrastructure, or simply provide "unforgettable experiences" for events in public spaces. "We're excited to work with a new launch provider, Skyroot, to help ensure access to space," Reflect Orbital Co-Founder and CEO Ben Nowack said in a statement. The first launch on this contract will use the Vikram-1 rocket and the second will use Skyroot's in-development Vikram-1U launch vehicle. The Vikram-1U has additional first-stage boosters and improved performance, the statement said. "We were recently licensed by the Federal Communications Commission to operate our first spacecraft, and we will continue to work with astronomers, local communities and regulators to earn the right to scale," Nowack said. In 1993, Russian scientists and engineers deployed a 65-foot mirror into orbit and sent a roving beam of sunlight on Earth. Though successful, the experiment named Znamya was shelved for want of funds. Reflect Orbital's plans have faced controversy as several environmental organisations have urged the FCC to scrap the permissions granted for the demonstration satellite. They argue that bright beams of light during the night might disturb wildlife, interfere with astronomy studies and affect circadian rhythms in humans.

stories.headline: Dining out: how safe is the food on your plate?
stories.deck: The rapid expansion of restaurants, food courts, and online delivery services has transformed Visakhapatnam’s dining culture. However, behind this convenience lies a major concern—food safety. Recent inspections across several restaurants in the city have repeatedly exposed stale ingredients, rotten meat, and unhygienic kitchens. As consumer complaints rise, Harish Gilai writes how the…
stories.bodyText:
Eating out is part of a routine for many in Visakhapatnam, whether it is a quick lunch between work commitments or dinner with family and friends. When people walk into restaurants, they expect the food to be fresh, the premises to be clean, and the meals to be safe. But what ensures these conditions are met? Behind every dish served at a restaurant, there is a chain of processes involved, from sourcing ingredients to storing them in a safe environment at the right temperatures, before hygienically preparing and serving them to the diner.
Much of the concern centres on what customers or diners cannot see — the hygiene practices followed inside restaurant kitchens. Recently, an online complaint about the quality of a paneer dish served by a popular restaurant, known for its exclusive vegetarian menu along the city’s Beach Road stretch, prompted the Food Safety team of the Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation (GVMC) to conduct a surprise inspection on October 13, 2026.
At first glance, everything appeared to be in order — the staff were neatly dressed, and the kitchen looked clean. But as the officials moved into the core kitchen area and pulled open the doors of the refrigerators and deep freezers, the picture changed.
Stored inside were several containers of cooked food — vegetable biryani, dal, rice, vegetable manchurian, and a variety of vegetarian starters, including samosas — that were stored at -18°C. The management allegedly intended to reheat the food and serve it to customers later.
The concern extends beyond food storage to how long it was stored and its quality. The team reportedly found gravies and some food items prepared the day before, while most of it had reportedly been prepared two or three days earlier. Instead of disposing of the stale food, the restaurant stored it for later use. According to reports, nearly 46 kgs of stale food items were found and destroyed on the spot by the officials. A case was registered against the restaurant under applicable provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and relevant rules and regulations.
The problem is not limited to one restaurant. A visit by the team to another establishment on the same lane, which opened a few months ago and became the new hotspot, raised similar concerns about food storage practices.
According to culinary enthusiasts, there is a long wait to get a table at this popular joint to savour its biryani, which costs ₹400 per plate. Yet a recent inspection allegedly revealed that chicken from the biryani was being stored separately in the refrigerator to be reheated and served with biryani the following day. Immediately after the finding, the team slapped a ₹70,000 fine and registered a case against the management.
The concerns raise a broader question about food safety standards across the city. According to food safety officials, violations are not confined to just a handful of small eateries. Medium-sized restaurants, high-end establishments, and even star-category hotels have come under scrutiny for their food safety standards.
Health and safety standards
To ensure these establishments maintain food safety standards, Joint Collector G. Vidhyadhari and GVMC Commissioner Ketan Garg have directed food safety teams to conduct surprise inspections at major hotels and restaurants across the city. In 2026 so far, cases have been booked against 128 hotels and restaurants, with fines totalling nearly ₹28 lakh imposed on the managements, according to officials.
The officials stress that stale food and poor sanitation are among the most common violations the teams come across during inspections.
GVMC Food Safety Inspector G.V. Appa Rao says that even highly rated restaurants have been found violating basic food safety practices. “The most recurring problem is the failure of restaurant management to estimate the quantity of food required for a day’s business. The tendency to cook more than demand often results in surplus food, and instead of disposing of it appropriately, some establishments store it for subsequent use,” he adds.
Drawing a comparison with household cooking, Mr. Appa Rao says families generally prepare food according to the number of people and try to finish it by the end of the day. “Restaurants, too, must estimate their requirements and ensure that surplus food is handled safely.”
“If a restaurant prepares food for 100 people but only 60 customers turn up, the remaining food should not simply be stored and served over the next few days,” he says, pointing out that the problem becomes particularly serious when the surplus consists of perishable items, especially meat.
He further points out that some establishments store cooked chicken for extended periods, until it becomes rotten. Prepared rice is stored for two to three days and subsequently used to whip up chicken, egg, and vegetable fried rice, posing a risk to consumers, he says.
“For example, in a recent raid, we found samosas stored in the refrigerator. Now, if those stale samosas are served to a child who loves them, without anyone knowing how long they were stored or how they were handled — what happens then?” he questions, underscoring the responsibility of food business operators.
Maintaining food safety requires more than proper food handling; the surrounding environment matters, too. In many inspected kitchens, officials reported numerous shortcomings in sanitation and basic infrastructure. Poorly maintained floors, damaged tiles and walls, a poor drainage system, and rusted knives and utensils in bad condition were observed. Most importantly, personal hygiene among kitchen staff is another major area where compliance has been noticed and recorded.
Water quality is another area that warrants attention. Mr. Appa Rao observes that some establishments use water supplied in cans without adequately ensuring its quality, while others depend on overhead tanks that are poorly maintained. Accumulated dirt and waste in such tanks can raise serious concerns about the suitability of the water for food preparation.
He recalls that during an inspection at a major hotel on the Beach Road, the team noticed that the kitchen was in a poor condition, particularly its drainage system. The establishment was also housing a poultry unit with around 40 to 50 hens close to the kitchen. The dust generated in the vicinity raised further concerns about the food preparation.
Another issue flagged by the officials is the use of food colours, other additives, expired products, and the repeated use of cooking oil.
Consumer grievances
Beyond inspections, complaints from consumers are another way in which food safety concerns come to light. Several complaints filed through online platforms and conventional channels bring to the fore allegations ranging from rotten chicken and improperly cooked food to the mixing of vegetarian and non-vegetarian items. Food safety teams stress that the most frequent complaints concern uncooked food, the use of spoiled chicken, and the mixing of vegetarian and non-vegetarian food items at several establishments.
For Jeevana, a resident of Murali Nagar, the reality of these hidden kitchen hazards hit home through an online food order. Despite paying ₹300 for the meal, she alleged that the biryani delivered to her was stale and unfit for consumption. The incident left her dissatisfied with the quality of food for the price and raised concerns about the quality checks followed by restaurants handling online food orders. She immediately contacted the food safety authorities through the ward sachivalayam.
From roadside stalls to compact takeaway counters, biryani outlets have become a familiar sight in several parts of the city. The area around the GVMC headquarters also has several such establishments, attracting hundreds of customers on a daily basis. Their popularity reflects the growing demand for affordable, readily available meals, particularly among employees, students, and people looking for quick dining options.
However, the expansion of these businesses has raised concerns about the conditions in which food is prepared, stored, and served. Poorly maintained kitchens, inadequate personal hygiene among food handlers, and the lack of proper sanitation facilities are among the issues that require closer scrutiny.
As food businesses continue to multiply, the enforcement machinery has struggled to keep pace with the expansion. The GVMC has only three food inspectors, highlighting the need to strengthen the workforce responsible for monitoring food safety standards across the city. With a large number of establishments spread across its jurisdiction, the existing staff face considerable pressure in responding to complaints, conducting inspections, and following up on violations.
Enforcement also involves responsibilities beyond conducting raids. Officials have to issue notices, pursue cases, and attend court proceedings in connection with violations. The absence of adequate supporting personnel, including staff to assist inspectors with court-related work and the service of notices, adds to their workload and affects the time available for field inspections.
Recognising this need for a wider enforcement mechanism, the GVMC has constituted Sanitation and Health Enforcement (SHE) teams across all 10 zones. There are currently 20 teams, with two teams assigned to each zone. Each team comprises a sanitary inspector, a sanitation secretary, a woman police personnel member and other staff from the ward secretariat system.
SHE teams
The teams have been tasked with carrying out inspections of food outlets and other establishments to ensure compliance with sanitation and hygiene requirements. They are expected to inspect at least two to four establishments every day in their respective zones, enabling the civic body to extend its monitoring beyond the limited number of food inspectors.
Assistant Health Officers monitor the overall functioning of the teams. Apart from identifying violations and initiating enforcement action, the SHE teams also undertake food safety awareness activities to sensitise business operators about the importance of maintaining clean premises, proper food-handling practices, and ensuring hygienic conditions in kitchens and serving areas. The teams reportedly impose fines amounting to at least ₹80,000 to ₹1 lakh every month for sanitation-related violations.
“The initiative is intended to strengthen ground-level enforcement and improve compliance among food businesses through a combination of inspections, penalties and awareness campaigns,” says Assistant Medical Officer of Health (AMOH), Gajuwaka Zone, S. Kiran Kumar.
Ultimately, ensuring food safety requires consistent attention to kitchen infrastructure, water quality, strict sanitation, and proper food storage. While taste and presentation are what initially draw a consumer to an establishment, it is what happens behind the kitchen doors that truly matters. Adhering to food safety standards must not be confined to inspection days; it must become an everyday habit for everyone in the food industry.

stories.headline: Georgia block party shooting kills two, injures dozens
stories.deck: Authorities do not believe there is a remaining ‌threat to the public, but have not publicly named any suspects or persons of interest, and have not identified a motive for ‌the shooting
stories.bodyText:
A shooting early on Sunday (October 4, 2026) at a Georgia block party left two people dead and almost three dozen injured, some critically, local and state officials said.
Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy told a news conference that two men, aged 21 and 23, were shot dead in Vienna, Georgia, about 135 miles (216 km) south of Atlanta. Thirty-five people were injured, mostly by gunshot wounds, officials told reporters.
They said hundreds of people had attended the event, which came at the end of Dooly County High School’s homecoming week.
Authorities do not believe there is a remaining threat to the public, but have not publicly named any suspects or persons of interest, and have not identified a motive for the shooting.
“We don’t want to presume as to what caused it,” said Chris Hosey, director of the Georgia Bureau of Investigation.
Those wounded range in age from 14 to 51, officials said.

stories.headline: Fees for professional courses can be hiked midstream only in exceptional cases: SC
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: In a relief to students pursuing professional courses like engineering and medicine in private colleges who have to face a fee hike midstream, Supreme Court has held that any change in fee structure after admission can be allowed only in exceptional circumstances.
While appreciating the contribution of self-financing institutions to the education sector, a bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe said there should be certainty regarding fees, and students must not be forced to pay more than that prescribed at the time of admission.
"For the overwhelming majority of households, the fee payable for a professional course constitutes a substantial part of the family's income and savings; it is not a matter of incidental expenditure. The parents make provisions for the fees... with the aspiration that their children will acquire better qualifications, secure better opportunities and build a future that may be better than their own. Many students and families also depend on educational loans to finance professional higher education," SC said, noting fees charged in professional courses are reported to be 711% higher than in general courses.
The court said it was a matter of good governance for the state and its regulatory bodies to create an ecosystem in which there was certainty about the financial obligation that students and their families need to undertake to acquire professional qualifications.

"Adverse variations in financial commitment, and the insecurities that it may create, will impact the student and the family, and, in the long run, have an adverse effect on the quality and character of the professionals in the making. We are of the opinion that it is not difficult to formulate a scheme through which such uncertainties can be avoided," it said.
SC quashed a 37% fee hike for BTech courses for the 2023-27 cohort at Dr BC Roy Engineering College in West Bengal. The college had also imposed a new development fee.
Passing an order in favour of students who had challenged the fee hike, the bench said, "The regulatory regime for fixation of fees, as contemplated in the decisions of this court, AICTE regulations, National Education Policy 2020 coupled with principles of certainty, necessitates the relevant authorities to notify fee payable for the entire course before a student takes admission... Variation is permissible only in exceptional instances such as unforeseen increase in the expenditure."

briefs.headline: Trump's new press secretary defends 'lawyer' title
briefs.deck: Appointed by U.S. President Donald Trump, Ms. Zacharia has described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media, and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit
briefs.bodyText:
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, under scrutiny over her legal credentials, seemed to acknowledge Thursday (October 15, 2026) that she had failed the bar exam, but argued she was accurate in presenting herself as a lawyer.
Appointed by U.S. President Donald Trump, Ms. Zacharia has described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media, and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.
But there is no evidence to suggest that the 41-year-old press secretary has ever passed the bar exam, required to obtain a license to practice law in the United States, after graduating from Pepperdine University with a law degree.
When questioned on Thursday (October 15, 2026) by conservative media outlet Real America's Voice, Ms. Zacharia said she had registered to take the bar exam but was then "distracted and overwhelmed" by plans to move with her husband to China.
"We just said, 'Let's take this time, and I'll take the bar and see what happens.' The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China, and we left shortly thereafter," she said.
In Beijing, Ms. Zacharia worked as a lawyer at a major Chinese law firm.
She explained that she didn't retake the bar exam upon returning to the United States due to the birth of her first child.
Ms. Zacharia said that "many people in the field" had assured her that she could "label myself a lawyer, not attorney at law...and provide legal analysis, not legal advice," given her law degree and experience in business law gained in China.
"I was very careful how I executed this," she said.
The Campaign for Accountability, a political ethics organization, on Wednesday (October 14, 2026) called for the California Bar Association to launch an investigation.
"In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn't puffery; it's a crime," the organization stated in a press release.
Ms. Zacharia held her first White House press briefing on Tuesday (October 13, 2026) with an unusually short press conference where she answered questions from three journalists.
She succeeded Karoline Leavitt, a loyal Trump supporter and often combative press secretary, who stepped down in August to care for her young children.

briefs.headline: The fuel frenzy: rising kerosene prices in Keralam
briefs.deck: Shrinking Central allocation and rising prices have left Keralam’s traditional fishers and ration-card holders struggling to secure adequate supplies of kerosene. Sarath Babu George examines the challenges of sustaining livelihoods and the hurdles in transitioning to cleaner fuels
briefs.bodyText:
Around 4 p.m. at the Vizhinjam fishing harbour on the outskirts of Thiruvananthapuram district in Keralam, dark clouds gather ominously over the sea. A sudden, intense downpour accompanied by lightning lashes parts of the district.
Around the harbour, fishermen linger, looking skywards and weighing their options. Some appear to be returning to shore in a hurry, seemingly heeding warnings of deteriorating weather. Others remain undecided, reluctant to lose another day’s earnings, while a few seem determined to venture out, despite the gathering storm.
They begin preparing their boats for departure, carrying cans of kerosene and petrol to refuel their engines. The decision to venture into the sea is never an easy one for traditional fishermen, whose livelihoods depend on the vagaries of weather, currents and fish availability.
But increasingly, another uncertainty has come to dictate their daily calculations.
For fishermen like Muthappan K.J. of Chowara, kerosene shortage has become an additional burden in an already precarious occupation. He says the price of kerosene has risen sharply in recent months, while declining catch and the need to travel farther into the sea have pushed up operating costs.
“Kerosene prices have climbed from around ₹103 to ₹157 a litre within six months. With the subsidised supplies available through Matsyafed outlets, the government-run cooperative, insufficient to meet our fuel needs, we are forced to procure the balance from retailers at higher rates,” he points out.
Despite the government announcing hikes in subsidies, delays in reimbursing the subsidy allocation to suppliers that could extend up to six months affect the supply chain. Under such circumstances, fishermen are increasingly forced to rely on the black market. Kerosene stocks brought in from Tamil Nadu are part of such “informal arrangements,” Muthappan says.
Johnny of Vizhinjam adds that changes in fishing patterns have led to higher fuel bills. Higher temperatures and the movement of fish into deeper waters have forced traditional boats that normally operate closer to the coast to travel farther in search of catches.
The immediate trigger for the shortage is the steady reduction in the quantity of subsidised kerosene allocated to Keralam by the Union government.
Keralam has traditionally depended on kerosene to operate outboard motors used by small fishing crafts. The subsidised fuel distributed through the public distribution system (PDS) has served as an important source of support for fishing communities, even as the Centre has sought to restrict kerosene consumption as part of its clean-energy transition.
A senior official of the Food and Civil Supplies department says the Centre progressively restricted the purpose for which the allocated kerosene can be used. Earlier, subsidised and non-subsidised supplies were available under different categories, and kerosene supplied through the Centre could also meet the requirements of the fishing sector.
Subsequently, the State was directed to use white kerosene specifically for fishing activities, leading to a separate arrangement under which Matsyafed supplied the fuel on a non-subsidised basis. A separate allocation of non-subsidised blue kerosene that could be diverted for fishing purposes was also discontinued around two years ago.
The annual allocation in this regard fell from 37,056 kilolitres (KL) in 2020-21 to 25,920 KL in 2021-22, 15,552 KL in 2022-23 and 7,776 KL in 2023-24. The allocation declined further to 3,120 KL in 2024-25 and 1,854 KL in 2025-26.

“The Centre’s allocation is now intended primarily for distribution through ration shops. However, the State government continues to earmark a portion of available quantity for fishing activities, considering the dependence of traditional fisherfolk on kerosene,” the official explains.
At the same time, the government finds the available quantity inadequate even to maintain the existing distribution pattern for ration-card holders, let alone meet the requirements of fishermen. While the rise in market prices has increased, the retail price of PDS kerosene also increased from ₹71 to ₹77 a month ago.
Keralam has approximately 36,000 outboard engines, the majority of which use kerosene as the primary fuel, according to the Fisheries department.
The department acknowledges the need to move towards cleaner energy, prompting schemes to facilitate the conversion of kerosene-operated outboard motors (OBMs) to petrol and LPG-run engines. An outlay of ₹1.95 crore was recently sanctioned for the initiative during the current financial year.
The scheme is intended to facilitate the gradual replacement of OBMs through subsidies. The department hopes that the transition will reduce maintenance and repair costs associated with kerosene engines, while lowering greenhouse gas emissions and environmental pollution.
However, in order to achieve its goal of phasing out OBMs, the government will have to overcome the wide perception among the fishing community that the Japanese kerosene-powered engines are more reliable when boats need to accelerate or negotiate choppy waters.
Fisheries officials point out that the hesitation among fishermen partly reflects misconceptions about the long-term advantages of alternative fuels. They plan to increase awareness of the benefits of petrol and other cleaner propulsion systems.
Matsyafed has targeted the conversion of around 200 fishing boats a year. The agency facilitated the conversion of 177 engines under the scheme last year, according to an official.
Jackson Pollayil, president of the Kerala Swatantra Matsyathozhilali Federation, says the fishing community is reluctant to take risks with expensive engine conversions without assurances that technical problems will be addressed. There are also concerns about the availability of LPG supplies and the role of intermediaries in determining prices.
Jackson adds the immediate priority should be to ensure affordable fuel supplies while the transition takes place. The federation has called for fuel to be made available at fair and affordable rates, exempt from the Goods and Services Tax, through existing Fisheries department outlets and without restrictive quantity limits for fishermen who depend on outboard and inboard engines.
The crisis extends well beyond the fishing harbours. The reduction in kerosene allocations has also disrupted supplies through ration shops, leaving households uncertain whether they will receive even their reduced entitlement.
During the financial years 2023-24 and 2024-25, the allocation of kerosene in PDS was significantly reduced, standing at 11,076 KL and 4,368 KL, respectively. Although the allocation increased in 2025-26 to 24,420 KL, the supply has subsequently nosedived.
For the October-December quarter of 2026-27, the Centre has made an allocation of 4,068 KL, much lower than the allocation of 5,676 KL in the previous quarter.
T. Muhammedali, general secretary of the All Kerala Retail Ration Dealers’ Association, says a sharp reduction in the allocation left many ration shops unable to supply kerosene to even half their cardholders.
Pink (priority households) and blue (non-priority subsidy), white (non-priority non-subsidy) ration-card holders receive half a litre of kerosene every three months, while yellow card holders under the Antyodaya Anna Yojana are entitled to one litre every three months. Besides, nearly 1% of families in the State which lack electricity are provided six litres of kerosene.
“The reduced allocation makes it difficult for dealers to ensure supply for all beneficiaries. For instance, a shop serving 800 cardholders may receive enough kerosene for only 400 people. Those who arrive first receive the fuel, while others have to return empty-handed. This has led to arguments with consumers at various places,” he laments.
The recent power cuts have also fuelled the demand for kerosene in Keralam. Despite the State’s near-universal electrification, interruptions in electricity supply have prompted some families, particularly in remote areas, to seek kerosene for lighting and other needs, ration dealers say.
It is estimated that Keralam requires a total allocation of at least 15,792 KL per quarter, comprising 9,600 KL per quarter for the PDS and 6,192 KL per quarter for the fishing sector to meet the current demand for kerosene.
Recently, Food and Civil Supplies Minister Anoop Jacob took the issue up with the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, but the State has yet to receive a favourable response.
The Centre’s position, he says, is that Keralam’s near-total electrification and high coverage of LPG connections do not justify an increase in the kerosene allocation.
The State has challenged the assessment by highlighting the continued demand in coastal and hilly areas, and among economically weaker sections. The fuel is still used for domestic purposes, including cooking, lighting and starting fires for cooking with firewood, according to the Minister.
He also argues that the Centre’s allocation does not adequately account for the requirements of coastal communities, who have been receiving kerosene under the distribution system for several decades.
However, despite the State’s strong pitch for greater kerosene allocation, officials concede that the demand would likely go ignored, considering the Centre’s broader policy to reduce dependence on fossil fuels and encourage cleaner alternatives. This push has intensified since India co-founded the Global Biofuel Alliance during its G20 presidency in September 2023.
Besides, as many as 21 States and Union Territories have become kerosene-free thus far, with efforts under way to achieve the objective across the country.
For Keralam, however, achieving the kerosene-free status remains a distant and challenging prospect. Despite the State government’s efforts to support the conversion of OBMs to alternative fuels, the scale of the task calls for substantially greater financial assistance with the Centre’s support.
Back at Vizhinjam, the decision to put out to sea still depends on the weather, the expected catch and the risks involved. Increasingly, however, it also depends on whether the boat can be fuelled at a price that leaves enough to sustain the crew.
For traditional fishermen, the transition to cleaner energy cannot be measured solely by the number of engines converted or the quantity of kerosene eliminated. It must also be judged by whether fishing remains a viable livelihood during the transition.
Until affordable alternatives are available at scale, the withdrawal of subsidised supplies risks leaving those who depend on kerosene caught between a shrinking allocation and a market they can scarcely afford.

briefs.headline: Mysuru Dasara: When tradition meets novelty
briefs.deck: Dasara has gradually evolved from a palace-centric celebration into a multi-venue festival encompassing culture, entertainment, youth engagement, and tourism. The inclusion of Kambala this year has brought in new questions, writes Laiqh A. Khan
briefs.bodyText:
In the bygone era, the conclusion of the Jumboo Savari on Vijayadashami would be followed by the Torchlight Parade at Bannimantap, with the Maharaja, on horseback, receiving a ceremonial royal salute from his kingdom’s armed forces and cavalry amid the glow of traditional torches.
Cut to the present, and spectators pour into the Bannimantap grounds and jostle for vantage points not only to watch motorcycle acrobatics and equestrian displays, but also to witness a drone show in which thousands of LED-fitted drones create formations ranging from the solar system and world map to tigers, peacocks, and Goddess Chamundeshwari.
The drone show, which has given a high-tech edge to the Torchlight Parade alongside traditional military and police displays, is just one of the many transformations Mysuru Dasara has witnessed over the years.
Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar, for whom the 2026 celebrations mark his first Dasara as the State’s executive head, has signalled his intention to introduce further changes. He has proposed inviting the Chief Ministers of other southern States and including their tableaux in the procession to give it a broader regional character. More controversially, he announced the introduction of Kambala, the traditional slush-track buffalo race of coastal Karnataka. This has drawn opposition from farmers’ groups, environmentalists, and historians, reopening questions about whether the expansion of Dasara’s cultural canvas strengthens the festival or risks diluting its distinctive identity.
Over four centuries
Dasara has a history spanning more than four centuries, with its origins dating back to the Vijayanagara empire. After its decline, Raja Wadiyar I formally instituted Dasara celebrations at Srirangapatna in 1610 before shifting to Mysuru after the fall of Tipu Sultan in 1799.
Over the centuries, the festival evolved into a distinctive expression of the region’s royal heritage, with the Wadiyars patronising religious rituals, music, dance, and other arts.
In view of the abolition of the privy purse by the then Government of India, which ended all official privileges and status of former princely rulers, the Maharaja of Mysore, since 1970, ceased to occupy the golden howdah atop an elephant during the Jumboo Savari and withdrew from organising the Dasara festival, paving the way for the Karnataka government to take over the responsibility of conducting Dasara as a “Nada Habba” or “festival of the region”.
With the idol of Goddess Chamundeshwari replacing the Maharaja in the golden howdah, the Jumboo Savari continued with traditional grandeur, with the cooperation of the erstwhile royal family. Other elements, including the illumination of the iconic Mysuru palace, music programmes in its forecourt, and Vajramushti Kalaga, a traditional form of wrestling involving knuckle-dusters, also continued alongside the Wadiyar family’s private Dasara, during which the erstwhile Maharaja ascended the golden throne and held a private durbar.
The Jumboo Savari, even without the Maharaja, continued to draw huge crowds in the 1970s and 1980s, when there were fewer competing attractions and much of Mysuru’s population turned out along the procession route. According to veteran Mysurean, writer and journalist Gauri Satya, the procession gradually acquired additional elements of pageantry, with tableaux joining the folk troupes, marching contingents and caparisoned elephants.
Expanding canvas
After 2000, Dasara gradually evolved from a palace-centric celebration into a multi-venue festival encompassing culture, entertainment, youth engagement, and tourism.
Yuva Dasara, featuring concerts by playback singers and rock bands from across the country, became a major attraction among young people. Performers such as A.R. Rahman, Sonu Nigam, and Shreya Ghoshal drew enthusiastic audiences over the years. Prabhu Deva was among the prominent performers at Yuva Dasara this year. As crowds grew, congestion around the Maharaja’s College grounds prompted the authorities to shift the event to a larger venue near the Outer Ring Road at Uttanahalli.
The administration also introduced Ahara Mela, or the food festival. Its popularity is evident from the nearly 700 applications received for around 100 stalls at this year’s Dasara.
Other additions, including an air show by the Indian Air Force’s Surya Kiran Aerobatic Team, Raitha Dasara celebrating agrarian culture, Mahila Dasara for women, Makkala Dasara for children, Kavi Goshti or poets’ meet, Dasara Book Fair, and Yoga Dasara, have broadened the festival’s appeal.
While these additions have attracted new audiences, Kambala this year has raised a more fundamental question about the cultural boundaries of Mysuru Dasara. Unlike drone shows or celebrity concerts, which primarily change how people experience the festival, Kambala introduces a distinct regional tradition into its programme.
Cultural boundaries?
Scion of the erstwhile Mysuru royal family Yaduveer Krishnadatta Chamaraja Wadiyar, who is also the BJP MP representing Mysuru in the Lok Sabha, has questioned the move, arguing that Kambala does not fit into Mysuru’s cultural milieu.
Congress leader in Mysuru S. Rajesh, meanwhile, contended that there is little justification for excluding Kambala when the festival already features art forms from other regions, including Kathak and Kuchipudi, as well as Chenda percussion from Kerala. Kambala, he argues, is a spectacular traditional sport that is part of Karnataka’s cultural heritage.
The Chief Minister also defended the decision to hold Kambala, which is scheduled to make its debut on a specially prepared slush track at Sathagalli on the outskirts of Mysuru on October 18 and 19.
His claim, made during the inauguration of Dasara, that the rulers of the Vijayanagar empire had a tradition of bringing buffaloes to the celebrations has been disputed by historian N.S. Rangaraju. A retired professor of ancient history and archaeology at the University of Mysore, Rangaraju said there was no historical record to establish this.
In a drought year
Opponents, including Parashurama Gowda of Parisarakkagi Naavu, have questioned spending a substantial sum on transporting nearly 400 buffaloes and their jockeys from Dakshina Kannada to organise the event in Mysuru amid drought conditions. Officials have estimated the expenditure on Kambala at ₹5 crore to ₹8 crore. Farmers’ groups have separately raised concerns over the use of several lakh litres of water for the event.
Rangaraju contrasted the expenditure on Kambala with the modest remuneration paid to folk artistes from different parts of the State, who participate in Dasara and their accommodation in basic facilities such as marriage halls. The controversy has not only brought into focus the historical and cultural justifications for introducing Kambala, but also the question of how resources should be allocated to new attractions and established traditional programmes and artistes.
Though Dasara has repeatedly adapted to changing times and embraced new audiences, technologies and cultural initiatives, the challenge before the organisers, it appears, is to ensure that innovations strengthen rather than overshadow the traditions that give Mysuru’s festival its distinctive identity.

briefs.headline: Maharashtra FDA resolves 72% of 13,857 complaints in three months; AI filters out over 11,000 invalid submissions
briefs.deck: Pune records highest number of grievances, while complaints against dark stores and quick-commerce platforms rise
briefs.bodyText:
The Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA) received 13,857 complaints through its online grievance redressal portal in the three months since its launch on July 14, resolving 71.8% of them. Separately, an artificial intelligence (AI)-based screening system rejected 11,491 submissions at the initial stage, filtering out grievances deemed invalid, misleading or outside the department’s jurisdiction.
Sharing the portal’s three-month performance report on Wednesday (October 14, 2026) FDA officials said the system was introduced to provide citizens with a single platform to register complaints, track their status and ensure time-bound action by the authorities.
The portal, complaints.mahafda.gov.in, automatically assigns grievances to the concerned officers and escalates unresolved cases to higher authorities if action is not taken within the prescribed timeframe.
According to the FDA, 4,068 complaints were escalated during the three-month period because the officers concerned failed to act within the stipulated time. The system also automatically generated 4,068 notices to the officials responsible for the delays.
Of the 13,857 complaints registered, 13,017 concerned food-related issues, while 840 were related to drugs.
AI screening to assess and reject invalid grievances
Explaining the portal’s AI-based screening mechanism, FDA officials said the system assesses complaints at the submission stage to identify potentially misleading, incomplete, vague or jurisdictionally invalid grievances.
The screening process uses predefined rules and departmental data to assess the likelihood of a complaint being genuine, without requiring human intervention at the initial stage.
Complaints lacking specific information, falling outside the FDA’s jurisdiction or appearing to misuse the grievance mechanism are not admitted. The system instead informs complainants of the reasons for rejection.
Officials cited instances where customers complained about delays in restaurant service or the provision of drinking water before alleging that the establishment served unsafe or substandard food.
Such complaints, when found to lack sufficient grounds for FDA intervention, are filtered out during submission.
In all, 11,491 submissions were rejected through this mechanism during the three-month period, separate from the 13,857 complaints formally registered on the portal.
Pune region received most complaints
Region-wise, Pune recorded the highest number of complaints at 4,519, followed by Greater Mumbai with 3,762 and the Konkan region with 2,551. The Pune region covers five districts, while Greater Mumbai includes Mumbai City and Mumbai Suburban districts. The Konkan region includes Thane and other districts along the Konkan belt.
Nashik, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Nagpur, and Amravati followed in descending order of complaints received.
In the separate district-wise breakdown provided by the FDA, Pune district recorded the highest number of complaints at 3,762, followed by Mumbai with 2,551 and Thane with 1,090.
Together, the Pune and Greater Mumbai regions accounted for approximately 59.8% of the total registered complaints.
Among the most frequently reported issues, unhygienic manufacturing and storage conditions topped the list with 4,052 complaints, accounting for approximately 29% of the total. This was followed by 3,536 complaints concerning foreign objects found in food products, representing 25.5%.
Other major categories included substandard or unsafe packaged food (1,817 complaints), expired or spoiled products (829), and suspected food poisoning or food-related illnesses (787).
Complaints shift towards dark stores and quick commerce
The FDA also reported a change in the nature of grievances received through the portal, with complaints increasingly focusing on dark stores and quick-commerce operations.
Officials said hotels, restaurants and eateries initially accounted for the largest share of complaints. However, according to the department’s assessment of recent trends, nearly 50% of complaints now concern dark stores and quick-commerce services.
The department attributed the shift partly to enforcement action against traditional food establishments, suggesting that complaints in those categories may have declined following regulatory intervention.
At the same time, the increase in grievances concerning quick-commerce operations has brought greater attention to food storage, handling and product quality in the rapidly expanding sector.
Officials said the changing pattern would help the department identify emerging areas of concern and direct enforcement efforts towards sectors attracting more consumer complaints.
Complaints peak during sale and festive periods
Month-wise data showed that the portal received 2,075 complaints between July 14 and the end of July, followed by a sharp increase to 5,412 in August.
The number declined to 3,810 in September, while 2,560 complaints were registered during the first 14 days of October.
The highest weekly volume was recorded during the week beginning August 17, when 1,564 complaints were received. The second-highest was during the week beginning September 28, with 1,391 grievances.
FDA officials suggested that the increase in complaints during August and September could be linked to major promotional sales and festive-season demand, when higher sales volumes may increase the risk of unsafe or substandard products entering the market.
The department said the portal’s automated monitoring, escalation and screening mechanisms were intended to improve accountability among officers while ensuring that genuine consumer grievances receive timely attention.

briefs.headline: Can't write off AT-1 bonds of Yes Bank worth Rs 8.4k crore: SC
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Thursday upheld a Bombay high court order which quashed a decision of the Yes Bank administrator to write off additional tier 1 bonds worth Rs 8,415 crore in March 2020.
A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Augustine George Masih said, "We see no reason to interfere with the impugned judgement. The appeals are dismissed."
"Putting the investors to such uncalled-for risk could have well been avoided. The purpose of the AT-1 bonds is imperative: it acts as a safety barrier to the bank from collapsing altogether. That purpose could have been served had RBI and Yes Bank acted in accordance with the terms of the Master Circular," the court said.

Congress questions MEA’s silence on proposed Rubio-Jaishankar meeting
briefs.deck: The Opposition party’s dig at the government follows remarks by U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor during an interactive session at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum
briefs.bodyText:
The Congress on Thursday (October 15, 2026) asked why the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) was “silent” about a proposed meeting between the U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, in Mumbai.
It was not surprising that the U.S. Ambassador to India, Sergio Gor, had provided more details on Mr. Rubio’s forthcoming visit to Mumbai, Congress general secretary (communications) Jairam Ramesh said.
“It is also not wholly surprising to hear him say that Mr. Rubio will meet Government of India officials in Mumbai. But what is quite extraordinary is his statement that ‘we expect the Minister Dr. Jaishankar to be joining us there along with other individuals’,” Mr. Ramesh said.
“Since when has the announcement of India’s Minister of External Affairs’s meetings within India been outsourced to somebody other than the official spokesperson of the MEA?” he added.
The Congress’s dig at the government followed remarks by Mr. Gor during an interactive session at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum here, where he said Mr. Rubio would meet Indian government officials in Mumbai.
“We expect that Minister Dr. S Jaishankar will be there along with other individuals from Delhi, who will make a trip up there to see him in Mumbai,” Mr. Gor.
“India gets to know from the U.S. Ambassador just as it first got to know from Mr. Rubio himself on the evening of May 10, 2025 that Operation Sindoor had been halted. Why is the MEA silent on the External Affairs Minister’s tryst with Mr. Rubio in Mumbai?” Mr. Ramesh said.
Mr. Rubio will first visit Samarkand in Uzbekistan, before travelling to Mumbai, and Jamnagar in Gujarat, from October 17-22, 2026.

briefs.headline: PAC grills Centre, States on ‘fraud markers’ flagged by CAG in SC scholarship schemes
briefs.deck: Committee Members question the Secretary, Social Justice and Empowerment Ministry, on why action-taken reports against points highlighted in the CAG audit had not been submitted; Ministry assures panel that the reports will be submitted in a month’s time
briefs.bodyText:
The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of Parliament on Thursday (October 15, 2026) grilled the Union government and several State governments over their responses to gaps, including “fraud markers”, in the implementation of pre- and post- matric scholarships for Scheduled Caste students identified by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
The PAC, headed by Congress MP K.C. Venugopal, is likely to move privilege notices against the Chief Secretaries of six States who were supposed to appear before it on Thursday (October 15, 2026) to explain the gaps flagged in the 2025 CAG report but failed to do so, The Hindu has learnt. Further, with the Union government responding to the gaps by saying the implementation burden was on State and Union Territory administrations, the PAC has given the Union Social Justice and Empowerment Ministry one month’s time to submit a detailed action-taken report on each of the issues flagged by the CAG.
In its 2025 report, the CAG audit had flagged a plethora of issues related to the administration of the pre-matric and post-matric scholarships for SC students. These included 40.75 lakh beneficiaries from as many as 14 States receiving scholarships with delays ranging from one to 90 months; over 3.5 lakh beneficiaries not receiving their scholarships at all; over 5,700 cases of scholarships being disbursed without proper checks of income eligibility; over 6,000 cases of non-SC beneficiaries receiving the scholarships meant for SC students; and issues related to beneficiaries receiving double payments, short payments, and excess payments.
During the PAC hearing on Thursday (October 15, 2026), the Chief Secretaries of Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka, Punjab, Odisha, Bihar, and Madhya Pradesh were supposed to appear for briefing the Members; however, none of the States had deputed the respective officials, sources told The Hindu. Further, the committee Members questioned the Secretary, Social Justice and Empowerment, on why action-taken reports against each point highlighted in the CAG audit were not submitted.
The Social Justice Ministry is learnt to have told the committee that since the implementation of the scholarship schemes rests with the State governments, it was unable to file action-taken reports as the respective State governments had not shared them with the Union Ministry. Upon further questioning, the Union Ministry has assured that the reports will be submitted in a month’s time.
Both the pre-matric and post-matric scholarship schemes are Centrally sponsored schemes, with the Union government sharing the financial burden on a 60:40 ratio with State and UT governments (90:10 for northeastern States). From 2017-24, a total of 52,878 crore was spent on these two schemes, of which about ₹30,234.5 crore came as the Union government’s share.
The committee went on to ask the Union Ministry why the CAG audit had shown continuing instances of fraud markers (such as same caste certificates being used by multiple beneficiaries in Uttar Pradesh, students in Odisha receiving scholarships in seemingly common bank accounts, and over ₹13 crore being paid in Haryana to beneficiaries where Aadhaar and bank details were not matching) if Direct-Beneficiary Transfers alongside the Aadhaar Payment Bridge System were meant to weed out dummy beneficiaries, as stated by the Union government.
The committee also pointed out during the hearing that the shift to the DBT method had resulted in significant drops in the number of beneficiaries in both the pre-matric and post-matric scholarships for SC students. It noted that despite time for recovery, the 2025-26 figures for the post-matric scheme had reached only 36.07 lakh beneficiaries against a target of 76.55 lakh beneficiaries.

stories.headline: 500 students join Bengaluru run to open up conversations on mental health
stories.bodyText:
More than 2,000 people, including around 500 school students, participated in the World Mental Health Day Run at Cubbon Park in central Bengaluru on Sunday, ahead of World Mental Health Day on October 10.
The youth-led initiative was organised by Imaan Zara Khan, a Grade 11 student at a private school in the city, and a 1M1B Changemaker. The event featured 3K, 5K and 10K runs and brought together students and runners in the city to encourage conversations around emotional well-being among young people.
The 3K category titled “Unspoken Run” carried the message, “A step for every conversation we never had,” with participants encouraged to see the run as part of a larger effort to make conversations around mental health easier to begin.
The event was part of Project S.A.F.E. (Student Advocacy for Emotional Well-Being), a student-led initiative founded by Imaan that focuses on adolescent mental health through research, storytelling and systems-level advocacy.
The initiative examines how signs of distress among young people are recognised, how they seek help, how adults respond and how schools can create clearer pathways to appropriate support.
“Through S.A.F.E., I want to move the conversation beyond awareness and ask a harder question: when a young person is struggling, what happens next? Who recognises the signs, who responds, and how do they reach the right support?” Imaan said.
Imaan will next present Project S.A.F.E. at the 10th 1M1B Summit at the United Nations Office in Geneva, where she will join youth leaders, institutions and stakeholders from across the world.

stories.headline: Engineers are architects of country’s future: Karnataka Minister N. Chaluvarayaswamy
stories.deck: ‘Use technology for social good; Innovation, technology key to building sustainable Karnataka’
stories.bodyText:
Water Resources Minister N. Chaluvarayaswamy said engineers are not merely builders of roads and buildings but architects of the country’s future.
He was speaking after inaugurating the 41st National Convention of Civil Engineering, organised by the Institution of Engineers (India), in Mysuru on Saturday.
The dedication and commitment of engineers were crucial to building a secure and prosperous future, he said.
While acquiring knowledge was important, putting it to use for the benefit of society was equally significant. Roads, bridges, water supply, electricity, and mobile technology had become integral parts of everyday life, but behind every such facility was the knowledge, hard work, planning, and responsibility of thousands of engineers, the Minister said.
He said the world was changing rapidly, with artificial intelligence, robotics, semiconductors, green energy, electric vehicles, and space technology transforming the way people lived. “Karnataka had a leading role to play in this technological transformation,” he said.
“There was immense talent, innovative thinking, and aspiration in every district, taluk, and village of the State. The responsibility of empowering these aspirations with modern technology rests with all stakeholders. Development is not limited to mega projects. Ensuring timely water supply to farmers, providing quality digital education to students, improving rural road connectivity, and creating skill-based employment opportunities for youth were also important indicators of real progress,” he said.
Technology should not merely be “smart” but also sustainable, the Minister said, urging youngsters not just to seek jobs but also to become job creators.
Recalling the contribution of Sir M. Visvesvaraya, the Minister said his vision and efficiency continue to inspire generations. Despite the limited technology available during his time, the projects he conceived and executed remain exemplary.
The Minister felicitated senior engineers for their contribution to the country and presented the ‘Young Engineer’ award to Manish Pandey.
Later, he interacted with engineers on the theme ‘Contribution of Civil Engineers Towards Building a Developed India – 2047’.
CIVDB chairperson P. Suryaprakash, office-bearers Sitaram, Nagaraj, H.S. Suresh Babu and Nanjayya, retired chief engineer Mahadev, and former All India Institution of Engineers president V.B. Singh were among those present.

stories.headline: From Egypt to Hampi: 8 Durga Puja pandals to visit in Bengaluru
stories.bodyText:

dhaak
, the waft of incense, the aroma of 
bhog
 and cotton-white clouds in the sky. This year, Maa Durga arrives in strikingly different avatars across Bengaluru — from an Egyptian-inspired pandal to a Hampi-themed mandap and idols rooted in traditional Bengali artistry. Beginning October 16, the city comes alive with rituals, music, food, festive cheer and performances rooted in Karnataka’s folk culture. Here are eight celebrations to add to your weekend plans.

When:
 Opens October 16

Mishor Mohamaya
 (Egyptian mystery). Egyptian-inspired décor will draw parallels between the civilisation’s reverence for the feminine divine and Durga’s associations with strength, motherhood and the triumph of good over evil. “We are celebrating this universal connection where two great cultures separated by time and geography are finally uniting under the reverence of Mother Goddess,” says association member Subhradeep Bhowmik.

 Sadumatadha Sadara Vidyabhivrudhi Sangha,

Shotodol
, a hundred-petal lotus symbolising purity, harmony and spiritual awakening. The theme also reflects the bond between Bengal, many visitors’ ancestral home, and Bengaluru, their present one. “It speaks about the universal feeling of protection, belonging and home,” says joint secretary Priyanka Sinha Roy.

- Evening performances

 For its 10th year, Anandotsab – Bellandur Durga Puja presents Mrinmayi Abhaya – Worshipping the Earthly Divine. sabeki
 Durga idol inspired by Kolkata’s Bagbazar Sarbojanin style, dressed in attire sourced from 
Krishnanagar, West Bengal. A

- Food and flea-market stalls
- Bhog on three days: khichuri on Saptami and Ashtami, pulao and paneer on Navami
Jayamahal Cultural Association: A classic Bengali Puja
Where:
 Ladies Club premises, Jayamahal Extension

 Opens October 16
Theme: In its 72nd year, the association celebrates Sabekiyana, a traditional Bengali style inspired by village festivities. The Durga idol will have an earthy clay finish, a simple Bengali sari, gold jewellery and a crown. Bengaluru-based artist Sumir Pal is creating paintings inspired by Sabekiyana and Kalighat pattachitra. “Our Maa Durga is going to be very simple, the way people celebrate in villages. That’s how we have depicted our Maa Durga this time,” says association member Dr Sharmistha Dutta.

briefs.headline: KSRTC to install 100 ADAS systems in buses across Karnataka
briefs.deck: The ADAS units will combine cameras, sensors, GPS and connectivity features to monitor both the road environment and the driver’s behaviour.
briefs.bodyText:
The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (KSRTC) is set to install 100 Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) in its buses to improve road safety, monitor driver behaviour and provide real-time alerts on potential hazards.
Recently, the Bengaluru Metropolitan Transport Corporation (BMTC) also announced plans to install ADAS technology in 50 buses as part of a pilot project.
According to KSRTC officials, the systems will be deployed across the corporation’s divisions in Karnataka, with installation and commissioning expected to be carried out between November 2026 and October 2027. The systems are expected to be installed at locations covering 17 KSRTC divisions across the State.
The ADAS units will combine cameras, sensors, GPS, and connectivity features to monitor both the road environment and the driver’s behaviour. The system will include a forward-facing road camera and a driver-monitoring camera, along with other cameras and hardware required for monitoring the surroundings of the bus.
A senior KSRTC official said: “The system is designed to detect several potential road-safety risks, including forward collision risks, lane departure, pedestrians, insufficient distance from vehicles ahead and other hazardous situations. It will also provide alerts to drivers through visual, audible, and buzzer warnings.”
“The driver-monitoring component will focus on identifying signs of fatigue and distraction. It will be capable of detecting drowsiness, yawning, prolonged eye closure, mobile-phone use, driver distraction and driver absence, among other behaviours. The system is also designed to monitor certain aspects of driver posture and attention while the bus is in operation,” the official explained.
The ADAS units will have 4G LTE connectivity and GPS/NavIC support, allowing vehicle and event-related information to be transmitted for monitoring and analysis. The specifications also provide for substantial onboard storage for recorded video and event data.
KSRTC officials said that the system will be linked to a cloud-based fleet management and analytics platform. This will enable authorised personnel to monitor vehicles, review safety alerts and access relevant video footage associated with incidents or detected events. The system is expected to support the retrieval of event-related video, allowing incidents such as sudden braking, collision warnings or driver-related safety alerts to be examined. The specifications also provide for driver-behaviour analysis and reporting.
The KSRTC tender requires the selected agency to be responsible for supplying, installing, and commissioning the systems in KSRTC buses at designated locations. The corporation has also specified three years of comprehensive warranty support, along with availability of spare parts for at least 10 years.
Officials added that the deployment is expected to give KSRTC access to data on both vehicle movement and driver behaviour, potentially providing officials with a broader picture of safety-related events across the fleet.

Bengaluru:
 A coalition of Bengaluru hospitality and liquor trade bodies has urged Bengaluru Urban deputy commissioner to relax dry-day restrictions proposed for legislative council elections, arguing that they would disproportionately affect thousands of businesses despite the limited electorate.
The district administration has proposed dry days from 4pm on Oct 21 to 4pm on Oct 23 and on Oct 27, when votes will be counted. It is yet to decide on the request.
The delegation sought permission for restaurants, hotels and bars to serve food and non-alcoholic beverages and undertake deliveries during the dry-day period, with liquor counters sealed and no alcohol sold or served. It also sought an end to counting-day restrictions by 4pm or immediately after results are declared, instead of midnight.
The delegation represented Okkuta, comprising National Restaurant Association of India’s Bengaluru chapter, Bruhat Bengaluru Hotels Association, Bangalore Hotels Association, Karnataka State Hotels Association, Karnataka Bakery, Sweets & Cafe Association and Bengaluru City Liquor Traders Association. The restrictions concern elections to Bengaluru teachers’ constituency and Karnataka South-East graduates’ constituency, where only registered teachers and graduates can vote.
 Okkuta said Bengaluru teachers’ constituency had 16,063 voters in 2024, while hospitality businesses across a city of more than 1.4 crore residents would be affected for nearly three business days.
Although the proposed order prohibits only liquor sales, food operations are often disrupted because of enforcement confusion, the associations said. They estimated losses of nearly Rs 500 crore. Bangalore Hotels Association separately said individual establishments could lose about Rs 20,000 or more daily, besides losses to employees dependent on business volumes.
The associations said restrictions would affect service staff, delivery personnel and suppliers while reducing state GST and excise collections. Citing a previous Karnataka high court order concerning a teachers’ constituency election, they sought explicit clarification allowing food operations while alcohol sales remain prohibited.
NRAI Bengaluru chapter head Ananth Narayan said a dry day should halt liquor sales, not restaurant operations. “Our humble request is to seal the liquor store on dry days and monitor that, instead of locking the whole place. A blanket closure costs the govt and restaurateurs hundreds of crores. We work 30 days a month and take home the profit of just a few. Losing 4-5 of those days is a complete drain,” he added.

briefs.headline: BMTC plans 200 mini-buses to boost last-mile Metro connectivity
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 With 
Namma Metro
’s operational network set to cross the 100 km mark with the expected opening of the elevated stretch from Kalena Agrahara to Tavarekere, the challenge of getting commuters to and from stations remains. BMTC is now planning to strengthen the last-mile connectivity by introducing mini-buses that can navigate narrow roads and serve residential neighbourhoods.
While the state govt has given the green light for 200 mini-buses, BMTC is likely to procure 100 7-metre-long buses and another 100 measuring 9 metres. The govt will fund their procurement.
BMTC managing director Raghunandan Murthy said the proposed 7-metre buses would have a seating capacity of 20-22 passengers. “These will be diesel buses. We will float a tender in the coming days after receiving the govt order. It may take around three months to induct the buses after the tendering process is completed,” he said.
The corporation is also examining the feasibility of introducing an automatic fare collection system on select routes. However, officials said it might not be practical on all feeder routes, particularly where bus stops are located close to one another.
“We will assess the feasibility based on the distance between the stops. On routes where the distance is longer, such a system may be viable. Most buses, however, will have conductors to collect fares from passengers,” the managing director said.
The mini-bus proposal was deliberated upon by multiple agencies, including Greater Bengaluru Authority, BMTC, BMRCL, city police and the Directorate of Urban Land Transport (DULT). Officials said DULT would study feeder-bus requirements across the network and recommend routes based on demand, taking into account both operational Metro corridors and upcoming stretches, including Pink Line. “Seven-metre buses will be deployed on narrow roads, while 9-metre or 12-metre buses will operate on roads that can accommodate larger vehicles,” an official said.
Officials said BMTC currently operates around 90 nine-metre electric buses, along with about 250 nine-metre Tata buses and 160 buses manufactured by Ashok Leyland. Many of its older nine-metre diesel buses, introduced from 2012 onwards, have crossed their prescribed operational limit of nine lakh kilometres and are due to be phased out.
BMTC had earlier operated nine-metre Swaraj Mazda buses, but these were eventually phased out. Officials said that while several manufacturers now produce 7-metre buses, most are used for school transport or by private companies for employee commutes.
BMTC had inspected 7-metre buses manufactured by different companies before drawing up specifications for urban services. The assessment covered seating capacity, headroom for standing passengers, floor height and other operational requirements.

briefs.headline: Karnataka govt yet to extend term of fee & admission panel
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru
: With the Karnataka Fee and Admission Regulatory Committee’s term ending Friday, the higher education department has sought an extension.
The committee holds the essential statutory mandate of reviewing institutional balance sheets, verifying infrastructure, and establishing non-exploitative tuition structures across private professional colleges in the state. Its presence acts as a safeguard to prevent commercialisation and shield students from unauthorised mid-term financial demands during active admission cycles.
With the higher education admissions season fast approaching, the committee’s decisions on fee caps and merit seat allotments are vital for maintaining equilibrium between private managements and aspiring student bodies.
Previous years have consistently seen dozens of student grievances regarding overcharging, making structural oversight indispensable during intense admission periods managed by authorities like Karnataka Examinations Authority (KEA). Tulsi Maddineni, secretary, higher education department, said, “We’ve moved the files seeking extension of the committee; the final decision has to be taken by the minister.”
Higher education minister Basavaraj Rayareddi was not available for comment.

briefs.headline: HYDGEN unveils 250 kW electrolysers at Mangaluru facility
briefs.bodyText:
Mangaluru: Singapore-based deep-tech startup HYDGEN inaugurated a manufacturing facility with an annual capacity of 20 MW at Ganjimutt in Mangaluru on Thursday, marking its Innovation Day 2026. The company also unveiled 250 kW anion exchange membrane and proton exchange membrane electrolysers designed to support hydrogen production for industrial applications. It plans to increase annual manufacturing capacity to 300 MW by 2029 and create local employment opportunities as operations expand.
Executive chairman and co-founder Dr Michael Geussens said the facility would allow HYDGEN to scale production and serve global markets. “This facility allows us to scale production significantly. Hydgen is not just built for India, it is built for the world to deliver practical, reliable, and cost-efficient hydrogen technology,” he said.
Co-founder and chief operating officer Dr Krishna Kumar said the company aimed to provide industries with a reliable hydrogen supply at predictable costs while manufacturing systems suited to the scale of Indian industry. 
Assistant vice-president of manufacturing Venkatram said 80% of the company’s products were indigenously manufactured. He also highlighted the development of a stack featuring what HYDGEN described as India’s largest active area.
Dakshina Kannada MP Brijesh Chowta and Mangaluru City North MLA Dr Y Bharath Shetty attended the event. Chowta said the company’s growth reflected the success of his ‘Back to Ooru’ vision, which seeks to encourage regional investment and development.
Shetty said on-site hydrogen generation could reduce logistics costs and ensure purity for industries. He assured support for HYDGEN’s efforts to promote domestic manufacturing and create jobs in the region.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru Jatre: City to host 10-day cultural festival from December 4
briefs.bodyText:
After the success of its one-of-a-kind Freedom Habba, Bengaluru will host a 10-day city-wide cultural festival — “Bengaluru Jatre” — from December 4 to 13, with the State government planning programmes across public spaces, educational institutions, museums, Namma Metro stations and other venues, Bengaluru Development Minister Krishna Byre Gowda announced on Saturday.
The event will bring together music, theatre, literature, food, art, heritage, and other cultural activities on a common platform, the Minister said, addressing the media here.
“Government agencies are expected to organise more than 100 programmes, all of which will be free to attend,” Mr. Gowda said, adding that a central website is planned to carry the festival calendar and connect visitors with individual programmes organised by participating institutions.
Mr. Gowda said the festival is being conceived on the lines of the traditional Ooru Habba or Jatre in Karnataka, where an entire community comes together to celebrate. He added that the government would adapt the idea to Bengaluru by allowing neighbourhoods, institutions, artists, businesses, and communities to organise their own programmes. “There will be no single Jatre ground and no single central stage. Instead, Bengaluru itself will become the stage,” Mr. Gowda said.
“Unity does not mean uniformity. Bengaluru has many colours and expressions. We want every neighbourhood, institution, and community to celebrate in its own way and still feel that it is part of one Jatre,” he said, pointing out that the event is intended to complement the government’s focus on civic infrastructure. “A government that works every day to address the everyday problems faced by citizens also has a responsibility to enrich the lives of people living in an increasingly mechanical and fast-paced urban environment, while preserving and promoting the State’s rich art and cultural traditions,” he said.
The five corporations can use parks and grounds for citizen-led activities, while the Tourism Department and Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation could use heritage sites for programmes and Bengaluru-specific experiences. Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Limited is expected to explore performances and busking at Metro concourses, while the Bengaluru Metropolitan Transport Corporation could carry the festival’s branding across its bus network. Schools, colleges, museums, galleries, science centres, cultural institutions and corporate campuses have also been invited to participate, Mr. Gowda said.

briefs.headline: Heavy rain snarls traffic, ride-hailing fares surge in Bengaluru

Heavy rain lashed Bengaluru on Thursday evening, leaving several stretches waterlogged and bringing traffic to a crawl.
Traffic congestion, particularly in the Central Business District (CBD), left many commuters stranded. Motorists on Hosur Road experienced bumper-to-bumper traffic, with several locations, particularly near Electronics City, reporting severe waterlogging.

briefs.headline: University of Liverpool opens campus in Bengaluru; 300 students enrolled
briefs.bodyText:
Around 300 students have enrolled across six undergraduate (UG) and two postgraduate (PG) programmes at the University of Liverpool. The campus was officially inaugurated in Bengaluru on Thursday.
According to details shared by the university, around 20,000 students applied for admission, of whom 300 were selected based on eligibility criteria such as English language proficiency and Class 12 marks.
Speaking to The Hindu, Tim Jones, Vice-Chancellor, University of Liverpool, said, “Bengaluru was our destination in India largely because it is a vibrant, entrepreneurial and technology-driven city. Our partnerships with universities and institutions in the city, including the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS), the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and Hindustan Unilever, are longstanding.”
Prof. Jones also pointed out that foreign universities opening campuses in India is advantageous for students. “Students will now have multiple options. Besides, it will reduce the cost of higher education abroad in terms of travel, accommodation and food. They can still pursue quality education while being close to their family and friends. There will also be student and faculty exchange programmes, with students from India travelling to the U.K. campus and vice versa,” he said.
The Bengaluru campus is small at the moment, and the university plans to expand the number of programmes based on student response and academic growth.
“The curriculum we are offering, the examination pattern and assessment methods will be similar to those followed at our campus in the U.K.,” he added.
To enhance students’ employability, the university has developed relationships with a number of industries and businesses in India.
Prof. Jones said, “We signed MoUs a year to 18 months ago with various companies when this campus was announced. Companies including Wipro, Unilever, Axis Bank and AstraZeneca represent a wide range of businesses based in Bengaluru. The whole purpose is to ensure we have strong employment opportunities for our students as soon as they graduate. We have also embedded the skills required by industry into our curriculum.”
